## TL; DR: AI Confidence Theater — Food for Agile Thought #551

Welcome to the 551st edition of the Food for Agile Thought newsletter, shared with 35,473 peers. This week, Elena Verna calls out AI confidence theater and asks teams to show real workflows, which pairs well with Teresa Torres and Petra Wille’s advice to start AI adoption with one messy to-do item. Also, Janna Bastow brings the same discipline to alignment meetings: clarify decisions before vague input becomes commitment. Anthropic frames Fable 5’s return as governance, while Alberto Romero questions the safety bargain, and Mike Cohn redirects failed Agile blame toward broken conditions.

Next, Aakash Gupta and Shubham Saboo treat PM work like code, while Hamel Husain extends that discipline to AI evaluation: track changes, show provenance, and make review paths obvious, and Tomasz Tunguz adds the cost pressure that will force selective adoption. Joost Minnaar reminds teams that rituals without shared power rot into theater, and Anthropic frames Claude Fable 5 as a teammate needing clearer boundaries.

Lastly, Ethan Mollick sees AI work shifting toward agent management, while Peter Yang expects model portfolios to reshape software economics. Charity Majors argues that leaders must support learning rather than demand unpaid adaptation, and Gergely Orosz reminds us that reinvention beats nostalgia. Finally, Abraham Thomas ties lasting progress to data quality that delivers real business outcomes by matching fitness for purpose with measurable value rather than relying solely on checklists.

## 🏆 The Tip of the Week

## Elena Verna : Please stop the AI Confidence Theater

Elena Verna suggests AI confidence theater is making everyone dumber and more anxious. Real value comes from useful workflows, honest outcomes, and maintained systems, not pretending agents run the company while prototypes need babysitting and hiring teams confuse polished vocabulary with actual competence. Show the work, or stop selling certainty.

Source: Please stop the AI Confidence Theater

Author: Elena Verna

## 🎯 Product

## Teresa Torres and Petra Wille : 🎙️ AI-Shaped Problems

Teresa Torres and Petra Wille suggest that AI adoption starts with one to-do item, not bigger problems, fancy tools, or perfect prompts. Their suggestion: Start small, expect bad results, and learn by doing.

Source: 🎙️ AI-Shaped Problems

Authors: Teresa Torres and Petra Wille

## Janna Bastow (via ProdPad ): How to Run Alignment Conversations Without Derailing the Quarter

Janna Bastow suggests that alignment meetings can derail quarters when vague input becomes an accidental commitment. State what is decided, name what is open, and send fresh ideas to the backlog instead of later.

Source: ProdPad: How to Run Alignment Conversations Without Derailing the Quarter

Author: Janna Bastow

## Hamel Husain : “It’s Hard to Eval” Is a Product Smell

Hamel Husain suggests that when AI outputs are hard to evaluate, the product design is broken: make provenance, checks, diffs, and expert-review paths visible so users can trust artifacts without redoing the work.

Source: “It’s Hard to Eval” Is a Product Smell

Author: Hamel Husain

## Aakash Gupta : GitHub for PMs: Version Control for Everything You Build With AI

Aakash Gupta and Shubham Saboo propose treating PM artifacts like code: store AI workspaces, skills, prompts, and evals in GitHub so teams can track changes, review work, and recover quickly.

Source: GitHub for PMs: Version Control for Everything You Build With AI

Author: Aakash Gupta

## 🧠 Artificial Intelligence

## (via Anthropic ): Redeploying Claude Fable 5

Anthropic depicts Fable 5’s return as a governance problem: stronger cyber safeguards, jailbreak severity scoring, and closer government collaboration now sit beside model capability in release decisions for everyone.

Source: Anthropic: Redeploying Claude Fable 5

## Alberto Romero : Fable is Back: This Safeguard Has Some AI in It!

Alberto Romero suggests Fable 5’s return signals a colder bargain: more safety theater, less useful coding, and deeper government control over frontier models. The bug was never the real story.

Source: Fable is Back: This Safeguard Has Some AI in It!

Author: Alberto Romero

## Tomasz Tunguz : When AI Costs More Than the Engineer

Tomasz Tunguz believes AI spending could become a serious engineering cost center, with 2029 scenarios forcing leaders to choose between token deflation, selective adoption, or AI bills rivaling payroll itself.

Source: When AI Costs More Than the Engineer

Author: Tomasz Tunguz

## Ethan Mollick : The twilight of the chatbots: How work changes along the exponential

Ethan Mollick suggests AI work is shifting from chatbot collaboration to agent management, where domain experts assign longer tasks, judge outcomes, and outpace organizations still writing yesterday’s AI plans today.

Source: The twilight of the chatbots: How work changes along the exponential

Author: Ethan Mollick

## Peter Yang : 18 Hot Takes On Where AI is Headed Next

Peter Yang proposes that AI is moving from costly frontier-only stacks toward model portfolios, super apps, agent-first products, and cloud collaboration, leaving traditional SaaS interfaces at risk of becoming invisible plumbing for autonomous work.

Source: 18 Hot Takes On Where AI is Headed Next

Author: Peter Yang

## ➿ Agile & Leadership

## Mike Cohn : We Tried Agile and It Didn’t Work

Mike Cohn suggests failed agile attempts usually reveal unchanged decisions, overloaded systems, and symbolic empowerment. Do not defend Agile; instead, ask what actually failed, then fix conditions around the work first.

Source: We Tried Agile and It Didn’t Work

Author: Mike Cohn

## Joost Minnaar (via Corporate Rebels ): Holacracy disadvantages: honest criticism and challenges of frameworks

Joost Minnaar believes Holacracy fails when companies copy its rituals without culture, turning self-management into disguised hierarchy. The framework helps only when teams adapt it, test assumptions, and share power.

Source: Corporate Rebels: Holacracy disadvantages: honest criticism and challenges of frameworks

Author: Joost Minnaar

## Charity Majors : In defense of AI mandates

Charity Majors suggests AI mandates are not automatically dumb management theatre: when change is urgent, leaders must fund learning, name tradeoffs, create cover, and stop pretending unpaid adaptation is strategy.

Source: In defense of AI mandates

Author: Charity Majors

## 📯 If You Can Facilitate a Retrospective, You Can Audit Your AI

Scrum teams inspect how the last Sprint went during the Retrospective. They are much less likely to inspect the work they have handed to AI, because no meeting on the calendar owns it. That gap is where a working AI automation quietly turns into risk: it keeps producing fluent, on-brand output long after the decision to trust it has expired. The AI Delegation Audit closes the gap by leveraging the facilitation skills teams already use in a Retrospective.

Thesis : The Delegation Audit is the missing inspection cadence for delegated AI work. It checks four things: whether the work still meets the standard, whether the model still fits the task, whether the team can still stop the automation, and whether reviewed assistance has quietly become unreviewed automation. You can try it on one workflow in fifteen minutes.

Learn more : If You Can Facilitate a Retrospective, You Can Audit Your AI .
